about:
A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY KANNADA EXAMINING OR LANGUAGE BODY. There is no widely-sat Kannada proficiency ladder -- core/exam-levels.json records kannada as exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial' -- so unlike Hindi, which at least has the Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha rungs to anchor against, there is nothing here to defer to. Karnataka's state school syllabi and the Kannada Sahitya Parishat examinations exist, but they are built for children schooled in Kannada or for literary attainment, not for an adult second-language learner against CEFR can-do descriptors, and neither was consulted. Read 'A1' here as the CEFR descriptor -- can greet, introduce oneself, and handle a short exchange in everyday spoken Kannada -- and as a measuring stick this project built for itself.

EXAM ENVELOPE: NONE EXISTS. There is no kannada/task-shapes/ and no kannada/mocks/, and no kannada/assessment.json -- the completion plan still lists writing one as an outstanding pre-A1 item. So unlike Hindi and Marathi, whose inventories could mine a checked-in mock for the exponent a paper item actually needs, nothing here can say which task demands which word. Where those files write 'the mock asks for X', this one can only write 'an A1 learner needs X'. That is a weaker claim and is stated as one.

SEARCH FOR AN EXTERNAL SOURCE: NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION. The project settled at HL-C287/HL-C290 that the proxy derivation is the method for tracks with no sat ladder, and the search was deliberately not redone for Kannada. Saying so is what keeps 'we did not look' from reading as 'there is nothing to find'.
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is the Instituto Cervantes Plan Curricular inventories. The proxy supplies the LEVEL and the shape of the columns; every Kannada exponent is this project's choice, and every point records which Spanish point or points it was derived from.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json
anchors.note: The DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Spanish is a proxy for LEVEL, never for grammar: each point was read as 'what must an A1 learner be able to do here', and the Kannada exponent that carries the same load was then chosen. Where Kannada carries the load with machinery Spanish does not have -- case suffixes, a dative subject, a zero copula -- the point is restated around the Kannada machinery and its Spanish origin recorded in derivedFrom.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), A1 descriptors
anchors.note: The spine already speaks CEFR (core/spine.json declares pre-A1 through C2) and core/exam-levels.json maps kannada onto it. Used for the functional column where the proxy's exponents are too Spanish-specific to transfer.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/kannada/ -- 268 lessons, 66 chapters, 362 schema-v2 knowledge atoms
anchors.note: Coverage is measured, not asserted. A point counts as covered only when every atom named in its probe is introduced by a lesson in this track. The atom set was re-derived from the merged tree after Kannada chapters 1, 2 and 4 were retired into the generator, because 37 of these atoms did not exist before that landed.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-levels.json, tracks.kannada
anchors.note: Records kannada as exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial', mapping 'cefr' -- and, unlike tracks.tamil, carries NO caveat. That absence is itself a finding: Kannada is as diglossic as Tamil, and KA-A1-REG-04 records the missing warning.

anchors.title: This project's unaided judgement about Kannada
anchors.note: There is no Kannada examining body to defer to. Every judgement in this file is the project's own and is attributable to nobody else.

notTransferred.why: The definite and indefinite articles and their contractions. Kannada has no article. Restated as an absence at KA-A1-DET-01, with ondu's indefinite use recorded separately at KA-A1-DET-02.

The exclamative que with adjectives and adverbs (que bonito!). Kannada exclaims with a different device entirely -- an intonation contour plus eshtu, or a bare adjective -- and there is no single word doing the job que does, so the point has no Kannada exponent to be enumerated against. Recorded here rather than as an untaught point, because there is nothing specific a tranche could be told to teach.

communicative-functions.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 54 A1 function points) and the CEFR Companion Volume A1 descriptors
communicative-functions.note: The proxy's functional column is finite and level-split, which is what would close a dimension -- for Spanish. It does not close this one, because the exponent that realises each function in Kannada is this project's choice every time, and a function inventory without its exponents is half a source. Kannada has no checked-in mock or task shape to pin an exponent against, so no note here can say which paper item needs a word.

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence, coordination and subordination columns)
grammar.note: THE DIMENSION THE PROXY HELPS MOST AND STILL DOES NOT CLOSE. Walking the Spanish grammar column surfaced demands no reading of the Kannada corpus alone would have raised -- an accusative for definite objects, an ablative for origin, the alla/illa split, ordinals. But four points have no Spanish origin at all and are flagged kannadaSpecific -- the human/non-human noun division, the one-suffix-per-job property of an agglutinating language, the p-to-h sound law, and the spoken/literary divide. Everything else in the case, postposition and register columns DOES answer a demand some Spanish point also makes, even where the machinery differs completely, and records which one.

phonology-orthography.source: the proxy's orthography columns, plus a direct character census of the corpus
phonology-orthography.note: The script column is the one place a count settles the question outright, and the count was taken rather than assumed: 42 characters taught by a script lesson against 69 used in headwords. Do not carry another track's shape here -- Tamil measured 52 of 52 taught, and Kannada measures 61%.

lexicon.source: the proxy's twenty notional-specific domains (A1-NE01 to A1-NE20) and its seven general-notion blocks
lexicon.note: The domain list is the proxy's and it transfers cleanly, because what a beginner talks about is not language-specific. Which words fill each domain is entirely this project's choice. The distribution is strikingly uneven and that is the finding: rural and natural-world domains are the best covered in the file, while shopping, money, transport, media and the arts are empty.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, and its `note` names what is missing so the file reads as a work queue rather than a score. Every atom named in a probe was checked to exist before this file was committed: a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and would be indistinguishable from real debt.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given in an introduction and used in address
points.note: hesaru and the frame nanna hesaru ... are both taught in chapter 2, and the frame is what an introduction actually uses.

points.label: place names: the town or village you are from, and the country
points.note: halli ('a village') is taught in chapter 55 and uuru ('town') nowhere. Not one settlement name, no word for a country, and no name of Karnataka or India is introduced anywhere -- so a learner can say what KIND of place they come from and never WHICH. The likeliest single fix is a chapter-55 sibling teaching uuru plus one place name.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
points.note: dina (day), raatri (night), gante (hour) and the season words are all taught. Kannada is unusually rich here because chapters 23-31 walk the whole day.

points.label: grammatical gender is not marked on the noun
points.note: Restated, not transferred. Spanish spends two points on -o/-a gender and on heteronyms like padre/madre. Kannada nouns carry no gender agreement at all; the fact an A1 learner must HANDLE is that nothing has to agree. KA-C05 teaches exactly that, from the other end: 'I speak' is the same for a man or a woman.

points.label: number: the plural suffix -galu
points.note: UNTAUGHT AS A MORPHEME, and it is one of the cheapest fixes in this file. -galu is already sitting inside five taught headwords -- bannagalu (colours), tingalugalu (months), kaalagalu (seasons), dehada bhaagagalu (body parts) -- so the learner has read it four times without being told what it is. One lesson naming it would convert every taught noun into a plural.

points.label: human/non-human is the division Kannada actually marks
points.note: Untaught. Kannada's real noun classification is not gender but human vs non-human, which drives verb agreement and the plural. Nothing in the corpus names it. NO SPANISH ORIGIN: Human vs non-human is the division Kannada actually marks, and it drives agreement and the plural. No Spanish point asks about it, because Spanish sorts nouns by gender instead.

points.label: qualifying adjectives before the noun
points.note: dodda, cikka, olleya are taught with the pattern itself: the adjective sits BEFORE the noun and never changes. That single grammar atom does the work Spanish needs three points for.

points.label: the adjective does not agree in gender or number
points.note: Restated. Spanish needs -o/-a and plural agreement; Kannada's adjective is invariant, and KA-C42's system atom states it.

points.label: age and newness as qualities of a thing
points.note: hosa (new) and haleya (old, of a thing) are taught, with the lesson explicitly warning that haleya is not used of a person.

points.label: relational adjectives: where somebody is from
points.note: Untaught. No gentilic, no way to say Kannadiga, Indian, or 'from Bangalore' as a property of a person. Blocked behind the same missing place-name vocabulary as KA-A1-N-02.

points.label: degree: intensifying an adjective
points.note: Untaught as a modifier of adjectives. tumba ('very') is not in the corpus. heccu ('more, a lot') and svalpa ('a little') are taught in chapter 58, but as quantity replies to an offer, never shown modifying an adjective -- so a learner can say 'more' about rice and cannot say 'very big'.

points.label: Kannada has no article; a bare noun is definite or indefinite by context
points.note: Restated as an absence. Spanish spends four points on el/la/un/una and their contractions. Kannada has none of it, and the A1 demand is that the learner NOT look for one. The zero-copula atom is the closest the corpus comes to teaching that Kannada omits what European languages require.

points.label: ondu ('one') pressed into service as an indefinite marker
points.note: ondu is taught as the numeral in chapter 7, but its everyday use as 'a' -- ondu pustaka, 'a book' -- is never shown, so the learner has the word and not the function.

points.label: the two-way deictic contrast: this one / that one
points.note: idu and adu are taught together in chapter 41. Kannada's contrast is two-way where Spanish is three-way (este/ese/aquel), so this one point carries A1-DEM-01 and A1-DEM-02 between them.

points.label: the i- / a- / e- system that generates the whole set
points.note: The strongest single grammar atom in the track: near is i-, far is a-, and the question is e-. Six words fall out of one pattern, and the pattern itself is taught.

points.label: place deixis: here and there
points.note: illi and alli, taught as members of the same i-/a- system rather than as two vocabulary items.

points.label: the mid-distance term Spanish has and Kannada does not
points.note: Recorded as untransferable rather than missing. Spanish aquel has no Kannada counterpart: the system is two-way. Nothing to teach; noted so the proxy point is accounted for rather than silently dropped.

points.label: first-person possessive: my
points.note: nanna is taught in chapter 2 as the word an introduction needs before it needs 'I'.

points.label: second-person possessive, and its respect grade
points.note: nimma is taught inside the question nimma hesaru eenu?, and the respect grading that makes it nimma rather than ninna is its own atom.

points.label: third-person possessive: his, her, their
points.note: Untaught, and blocked behind the missing third-person pronouns at KA-A1-PRON-03. avana / avala / avara cannot be taught before avanu / avalu / avaru are.

points.label: cardinal numerals one to ten
points.note: All ten are taught, one word per lesson, across chapter 7.

points.label: cardinal numerals eleven to twenty
points.note: The teens and twenty are taught in chapter 20 as additive 'ten-echo' compounds rather than as twenty separate words.

points.label: the written digits
points.note: All ten Kannada digits have their own script lesson, spread across chapters 9-18 so each rides behind a word already learned.

points.label: asking how many or how much
points.note: eshtu is taught inside the age question 'ninna vayassu eshtu?', which is the frame that carries it.

points.label: relative quantity: more, less, a little
points.note: svalpa, heccu and kadime are taught in chapter 58 as the replies an offer of food needs.

points.label: sufficiency: enough, that's all
points.note: saaku ('enough') and ashtee ('that's all') are both taught, and between them they close a refusal politely.

points.label: ordinal numerals to tenth
points.note: Untaught. Kannada forms ordinals with -aneya on the cardinal (mooraneya, 'third'), so all ten follow from one suffix on numbers already taught -- another high points-per-word target.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: Untaught. dodda and cikka give size as a quality, but there is no unit of distance, weight or length anywhere in the corpus.

points.label: first-person subject pronoun
points.note: naanu is taught in chapter 3, with its Proto-Dravidian pedigree and the explicit warning that it is NOT cousin to English me.

points.label: second-person subject pronoun, familiar and respectful
points.note: niinu and niivu are taught together with the rule that makes the choice: respect is the plural.

points.label: third-person subject pronouns: he, she, they
points.note: UNTAUGHT, AND THE LARGEST SINGLE HOLE IN THE GRAMMAR. avanu, avalu, adu and avaru appear nowhere in the corpus. A learner can talk about themselves and to one other person, and cannot say one word about anybody who is not in the room -- which also blocks KA-A1-POS-03, most of the family vocabulary from being used in a sentence, and every third-person verb form.

points.label: pro-drop: the verb ending already carries the person
points.note: Taught twice and from both ends: chapter 3 says naanu is usually left out, and chapter 5 shows why -- the -eene ending IS 'I'.

points.label: the dative subject: the experiencer is not the subject
points.note: This is Kannada's answer to gustar, and the corpus teaches it properly: nanage kannada gottu, with the whole 'knowing happens TO you' argument and the four Dravidian sisters lined up. Spanish reaches this through an indirect-object pronoun; Kannada reaches it through case, and the point is restated around the case.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: who, what, where
points.note: yaaru, eenu and elli are all taught, and chapter 41 shows them as the e- arm of one system rather than three separate words.

points.label: object pronouns
points.note: Untaught. Kannada makes them by putting the pronoun in the accusative (nannannu, 'me'), and no accusative is taught anywhere -- see KA-A1-CASE-03.

points.label: the reflexive, and the self-benefactive verb ending
points.note: Partially, and from an unexpected direction. Kannada's -ko ending means 'do it for yourself', and it is taught inside arthamaadiko ('understand') and tegeduko ('take'). A reflexive pronoun is not taught, but the self-directed verb is, which is the load Spanish se carries at A1.

points.label: place deictics
points.note: illi and alli, from the deixis system.

points.label: time deictics: now, later, soon, still
points.note: iiga (now), aameele (afterwards), beega (soon) and innuu (still) are taught in chapters 50 and 64.

points.label: today, yesterday, tomorrow
points.note: PARTIAL AND ODDLY SHAPED. naale ('tomorrow') is taught only inside the farewell naale sigoona, and naadiddu ('the day after tomorrow') is taught as its own word in chapter 50 -- but 'today' (indu) and 'yesterday' (ninne) are both untaught. The learner can name the day after tomorrow and not today.

points.label: manner: well
points.note: cennaagi is taught, and taught as an adverb -- the -aagi suffix that makes it one is part of the etymology atom.

points.label: polarity: yes and no
points.note: haudu and illa, chapter 1, taught as a pair.

points.label: additive: also, too
points.note: kuuda ('also, too') is taught in chapter 64. It is the nearest thing in the whole corpus to a joining word, and it is an adverb, not a conjunction -- see the KA-A1-CJ column.

points.label: manner deictic: like this, that way
points.note: haage ('that way, just so') is taught in chapter 49, and belongs to the same a- arm as adu and alli.

points.label: interrogative adverb: how
points.note: heege is taught in chapter 3 with the whole e- question family named around it.

points.label: the negative counterpart: not also, neither
points.note: Untaught. Kannada has no taught way to say 'me neither', which at A1 is a common turn in exactly the short exchanges this level is about.

points.label: the three-piece verb: stem, tense bead, person ending
points.note: The single most load-bearing grammar atom in the track, and it is taught twice -- chapter 5 builds maatanaaduttene from stem + -utt- + -eene, and chapter 32 names the machine outright.

points.label: present tense, first person
points.note: maatanaaduttene ('I speak') is built in full, and the sentence naanu kannada maatanaaduttene is the chapter-5 payoff.

points.label: the verb of being and existing
points.note: iru is taught twice over -- chapter 5 for 'to be / stay / live', chapter 32 as the frame the whole verb system hangs on.

points.label: the zero copula: 'is' is simply absent
points.note: Restated around Kannada. Spanish spends three points on ser/estar and the attribute; Kannada's equivalent demand is the opposite one -- notice that nothing is there. nanna hesaru ... is taught with the absence named.

points.label: a noun plus maadu builds a new verb
points.note: kelasa maadu ('work-do') and sahaaya maadu ('help-do') are both taught, and the pattern itself is an atom -- which is how one verb multiplies into many.

points.label: everyday verbs: go, come, see, eat
points.note: Chapter 32 teaches four core verbs as the beads the tense machine runs on, not as isolated vocabulary.

points.label: verbs of literacy and thought: read, write, understand, think
points.note: oodu, bare, arthamaadiko and yoocisu, all in chapter 33.

points.label: verbs of exchange: ask, hear, take, help
points.note: keelu is taught doing two jobs at once -- ask and hear -- which is a genuine Kannada fact rather than a gloss convenience.

points.label: the citation form is not the stem the endings attach to
points.note: Kannada's answer to the infinitive point. baa is how you name the verb; baru- is what the beads attach to, and chapter 32 teaches the difference explicitly.

points.label: the affirmative imperative, second person
points.note: Eight imperatives across chapters 43 and 44 -- baa, kodu, kulituko, nillu, keelu, noodu, maataadu, bare. Kannada's bare imperative is the stem, so these are free once the verbs are known.

points.label: the respectful imperative
points.note: kshamisi is itself a respectful imperative, and dayavittu is the softener that fronts one. The corpus teaches the polite form before the plain one, which is the right order for a guest.

points.label: a word that behaves like a verb but has no stem, tense or person
points.note: gottu ('known') is taught as exactly that oddity, and it is the predicate the dative subject needs.

points.label: the participle that chains one action to the next
points.note: Kannada's answer to the gerund. hoogi baruttene is 'having gone, I come back', and chapter 4 teaches the -i participle as the joint.

points.label: the past participle as an independent form
points.note: Untaught as a form in its own right. It is visible inside dayavittu ('having placed') and hoogi ('having gone'), but no lesson names it or builds one.

points.label: present tense with the -utt- bead
points.note: Taught in chapter 5 and named as a bead in chapter 32.

points.label: past tense with the -d- bead
points.note: Chapter 32 teaches tinde ('I ate'). Spanish spends three points on preterite paradigms and strong stems; Kannada needs one bead, so the three collapse into this.

points.label: the present covers the future too
points.note: A genuine Kannada fact the corpus is careful about: -utt- carries the future as well, and the separate -uv- future survives mainly in writing. Taught in chapter 32.

points.label: person endings across the paradigm
points.note: PARTIAL, AND UNEVENLY SO. The first person -eene is taught thoroughly. Third-person -aane / -aale / -aare are shown once, in passing, in chapter 5's grammar lens, and are not atoms -- and with no third-person pronoun to pair them with (KA-A1-PRON-03) they cannot be used.

points.label: the perfect: an action completed and still relevant
points.note: Untaught. Kannada builds it with the -iddu participle plus iru, both of whose parts are taught, so the construction is closer than it looks.

points.label: the imperfect: describing a past state or habit
points.note: Untaught. No past form of iru (ittu, iddenu) appears anywhere, so the learner cannot say what anything WAS.

points.label: the dative -ge: to, for
points.note: Chapter 6 teaches -ge with both its shapes (-ige, -kke) and the sound change behind them.

points.label: one suffix per job: Kannada stacks where Latin fuses
points.note: The structural fact an A1 learner needs about a case language they can actually see the seams of. Taught as its own atom. NO SPANISH ORIGIN: One visible suffix per job. A property of an agglutinating language that a fusional one cannot pose as a question.

points.label: the accusative -annu: marking a definite object
points.note: UNTAUGHT, AND A BLOCKER. Spanish's A1-SV-04 is about the personal a; Kannada's equivalent is -annu, which is what makes 'I saw the man' possible and what object pronouns are built from. Nothing teaches it, so every taught transitive verb can only take a bare object.

points.label: the genitive -a: whose
points.note: Untaught as a suffix, though its output is taught twice: nanna and nimma ARE genitives. Naming the suffix would let the learner build a possessive from any noun they know.

points.label: the locative -alli: in, at
points.note: Taught in chapter 5, and taught as the structural point rather than a word: 'in' comes AFTER the noun, glued to its end.

points.label: the instrumental: with, by means of
points.note: Untaught. -inda appears nowhere.

points.label: the ablative: from where
points.note: Untaught, and it is what 'Where are you from?' needs. -inda again, in its other job. With KA-A1-N-02's missing place names, origin is unsayable twice over.

points.label: the vocative: calling somebody
points.note: Untaught. No form of address beyond a bare name is taught, and no honorific like -avare.

points.label: Kannada puts its relators AFTER the noun
points.note: The single most portable structural fact between Kannada and English, and chapter 5 states it: 'Bangalore-in I am', the verb last.

points.label: relative position: near, far, on, under, inside
points.note: Untaught, entirely. Not one spatial relator -- mele, kelage, olage, hattira -- is in the corpus, so nothing can be located relative to anything else.

points.label: movement towards and away
points.note: Untaught. hoogu and baa give the motion; the destination cannot be attached to them.

points.label: before and after in time
points.note: Half. aameele ('afterwards') is taught as an adverb in chapter 64; the postpositions munce and nantara, which would let one event be placed relative to another, are not.

points.label: illa: the everyday no
points.note: Chapter 1, paired with haudu.

points.label: Dravidian negates by being, not with a not-word
points.note: The structural point, and the corpus teaches it properly: pustaka ide / pustaka illa. illa is the negative verb of existence, not a particle bolted onto a positive sentence.

points.label: illa as a full sentence answer
points.note: Taught, and its family spread is taught with it -- Tamil illai and Malayalam illa share the root, Telugu does not.

points.label: refusing an offer politely
points.note: beeda ('no thank you, I don't want it') is taught in chapter 58, which is the negation an A1 guest actually needs at a table.

points.label: alla: negating an equation rather than an existence
points.note: UNTAUGHT, and the pair is broken without it. Kannada splits negation two ways -- illa denies that something EXISTS, alla denies that something IS something else ('idu pustaka alla', 'this is not a book'). Only half the pair is in the corpus, so the learner can deny existence and cannot contradict a description.

points.label: yes-or-no questions
points.note: Partially structural. The -aa question particle is visible in heegiddiiraa and the echo-answer pattern is taught with haudu, but no lesson names -aa as the thing that turns any statement into a question -- which would be one atom for unlimited questions.

points.label: questions with an asking word
points.note: eenu, yaaru, elli and heege are all taught, and the e- system links them.

points.label: asking somebody's name
points.note: The chapter-2 payoff, taught with its familiar variant alongside.

points.label: asking how somebody is
points.note: niivu heegiddiiraa?, with the respectful and familiar forms both taught and the rule that picks between them.

points.label: asking somebody's age
points.note: ninna vayassu eshtu?, taught as a frame in chapter 19.

points.label: asking when
points.note: Untaught. yaavaaga is missing, and it is the one member of the e- question family the corpus never completes.

points.label: asking why
points.note: Untaught. yaake is missing, which also means no reason can be asked for -- and, with KA-A1-CJ-05, none can be given.

points.label: asking which one out of several
points.note: Untaught. yaava is missing, so a choice cannot be put to somebody.

points.label: asking where somebody is from
points.note: Untaught, and blocked twice: no ablative case (KA-A1-CASE-07) and no place names (KA-A1-N-02). This is a standard A1 exam item in every published inventory, and Kannada cannot form it at all.

points.label: the verb goes last
points.note: Taught and re-taught: 'I Kannada speak', 'Bangalore-in I am'.

points.label: a sentence with no verb at all
points.note: Two of them, and the corpus is proud of both: nanna hesaru ... and nanage kannada ishta, 'I like Kannada', which chapter 34 points out has no verb anywhere in it.

points.label: declaratives, affirmative and negative
points.note: Both halves taught, in chapters 5 and 1.

points.label: existence and non-existence
points.note: ide / illa is the pair Spanish reaches with hay, and chapter 1 teaches it as a pair.

points.label: the experiencer construction as a sentence pattern
points.note: Taught twice with two different predicates -- gottu and ishta -- which is what makes it a pattern rather than a phrase.

points.label: agreement between subject and verb ending
points.note: Taught for the first person. See KA-A1-T-04 for what is missing.

points.label: a noun phrase with an adjective in it
points.note: Chapter 42 teaches the position and the invariance together.

points.label: a relative clause modifying a noun
points.note: Untaught. Kannada relativises with a participle before the noun, and no such construction appears in the corpus. Three Spanish A1 points land here and none of them transfers.

points.label: joining two nouns: and
points.note: UNTAUGHT. Kannada joins nouns by suffixing -uu to each (naanuu niivuu) or with mattu between them. NEITHER IS IN THE CORPUS -- mattu appears zero times in 268 lessons and zero times in the generated book. A learner who knows 130 nouns cannot name two of them in one breath.

points.label: joining with but
points.note: UNTAUGHT. aadare appears zero times anywhere in the track. This also blocks A1-F2-09, offering a counter-argument, which is a function point in its own right.

points.label: joining with or
points.note: UNTAUGHT. athavaa appears zero times anywhere in the track. This also blocks A1-F3-02, asking about a preference by offering alternatives -- you cannot offer a choice without a word for 'or'.

points.label: negative coordination: neither ... nor
points.note: Untaught, and downstream of KA-A1-CJ-01: Kannada builds it on the same -uu suffix plus a negative.

points.label: causal clauses: because
points.note: UNTAUGHT. eekendare appears zero times. With yaake also missing (KA-A1-Q-07), a reason can be neither asked for nor given anywhere in the course.

points.label: purpose clauses: in order to
points.note: Untaught. Kannada uses the -alu infinitive, which no lesson forms.

points.label: simultaneity: when
points.note: Untaught. Kannada uses the -aaga participle, which no lesson forms; and yaavaaga is missing too (KA-A1-Q-06).

points.label: a clause as the object of a verb of saying or thinking
points.note: UNTAUGHT, and it is the reason yoocisu ('to think', chapter 33) cannot yet take an opinion as its object. Kannada uses the quotative anta / endu, and both appear zero times in the corpus. Three Spanish points land here, including A1-F2-02, giving an opinion -- the single most-used A1 function there is.

points.label: the -i participle as the joint between two actions
points.note: THE ONE COVERED POINT IN THIS COLUMN. hoogi baruttene chains two verbs with the -i participle, and chapter 4 teaches the joint itself. Kannada's real clause-chaining machinery is participial rather than conjunctional, so this is not a consolation prize -- it is the door the rest of the column opens through.

points.label: discourse connectives: in that case, afterwards
points.note: haagaadare ('in that case'), aameele ('afterwards') and kuuda ('also') are taught in chapter 64. They connect TURNS, not clauses -- which is why chapter 64 is named JOIN and still leaves this column at two of ten. Recorded as covered because the A1 discourse function is real and met; recorded here rather than in the function column because it is what the corpus offers in place of conjunctions.

points.label: identify oneself by name
points.note: nanna hesaru ..., the chapter-2 payoff.

points.label: ask for somebody's name
points.note: nimma hesaru eenu?, with the familiar variant taught beside it.

points.label: give your age
points.note: The question is taught (chapter 19) and the answer is not: no lesson shows a number used as an age, and the numbers stop at twenty.

points.label: ask somebody's age
points.note: ninna vayassu eshtu?

points.label: say where you are from
points.note: Unsayable. See KA-A1-Q-09 -- no ablative, no place names.

points.label: say what language you speak
points.note: naanu kannada maatanaaduttene, taught in full as the chapter-5 payoff.

points.label: confirm or deny what was just said
points.note: haudu and illa, plus the Dravidian echo-answer habit that makes a bare yes sound curt.

points.label: ask for confirmation with a tag
points.note: Untaught. Kannada tags with alva? -- built on alla, which is itself untaught (KA-A1-NEG-05).

points.label: say you know something
points.note: nanage kannada gottu, taught with the whole dative-subject argument behind it.

points.label: say you do not know something
points.note: Untaught. It needs gottilla, the negative of gottu -- one lesson away, since both halves are taught.

points.label: ask whether somebody knows something
points.note: Untaught. Needs the -aa question particle on gottu (KA-A1-Q-01), which is never named.

points.label: give an opinion
points.note: Untaught, and structurally blocked: it needs the quotative (KA-A1-CJ-08) so that yoocisu can take a clause.

points.label: agree
points.note: sari ('okay, correct') from chapter 1 and nija ('true') from chapter 49.

points.label: disagree
points.note: Untaught. Needs alla or a negated verb; neither is available.

points.label: express certainty
points.note: khandita ('certainly'), chapter 49.

points.label: express possibility or doubt
points.note: bahushah ('perhaps'), chapter 49.

points.label: evaluate something as good or bad
points.note: olleya ('good') as an adjective and cennaagi ('well') as an adverb. No word for 'bad' is taught anywhere, which is why the evaluation is one-sided.

points.label: say you can do something
points.note: Untaught. Kannada uses baruttade or -alu saadhya; neither is in the corpus.

points.label: say what you like
points.note: nanage kannada ishta -- taught as a sentence with no verb in it, which is exactly the point.

points.label: ask what somebody likes
points.note: Untaught. The frame exists; the question particle to turn it around does not.

points.label: say what you want
points.note: Untaught in the affirmative. beeku ('want') is absent, though its negative beeda ('don't want') IS taught in chapter 58 -- the corpus teaches the refusal without the request.

points.label: refuse something offered
points.note: beeda, chapter 58.

points.label: express a preference between alternatives
points.note: Untaught, and blocked by the missing 'or' (KA-A1-CJ-03).

points.label: talk about plans and intentions
points.note: Untaught. There is no distinct future form taught (KA-A1-T-03 notes -utt- covers it), and no lesson uses it for an intention.

points.label: give a direct instruction
points.note: The chapter 43-44 imperatives.

points.label: soften a request
points.note: dayavittu is taught as the softener and, importantly, with its register: when a Kannada speaker actually uses it and when they do not.

points.label: ask for help
points.note: sahaaya maadu is taught; the imperative sahaaya maadi follows from the chapter 43-44 pattern.

points.label: ask for an object
points.note: kodu ('give') is taught as an imperative in chapter 43. Without the accusative (KA-A1-CASE-03) the thing asked for stays bare, which is acceptable in speech.

points.label: ask for permission
points.note: anumati ('permission') is taught as a noun in chapter 65. The construction that requests it is not, so this is the word without the move.

points.label: respond to a request
points.note: sari accepts and beeda declines. Both are taught, which closes the pair.

points.label: offer or invite
points.note: Untaught as a move. Chapter 52's welcome vocabulary (door, chair, flower, garland) sets the scene for a guest without giving the sentence that invites one in.

points.label: greet
points.note: namaskaara, chapter 1, taught with the gesture that is the word.

points.label: respond to a greeting
points.note: namaskaara answers namaskaara; the lesson says so explicitly.

points.label: greet by time of day
points.note: shubhoodaya, shubha sanje, shubha madhyaahna and shubha raatri -- all four, one per chapter across 25-31, each with a note on how much they are really used.

points.label: introduce yourself
points.note: The name frame plus santoosha to close it.

points.label: respond to an introduction
points.note: santoosha, taught with the fact that Kannada borrows even this from Sanskrit where Tamil keeps a native word.

points.label: thank
points.note: dhanyavaada, and the lesson is honest that everyday Kannada often reaches for English 'thanks' instead.

points.label: respond to thanks
points.note: paravaagilla, taught in chapter 3 as the gracious reply.

points.label: apologise
points.note: kshamisi, with its register taught alongside it.

points.label: take leave
points.note: Three ways to part, none of them a blunt goodbye -- the whole of chapter 4.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: Untaught. No vocative, no honorific -avare, and no title. See KA-A1-CASE-08.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: Untaught. abhinandane is absent.

points.label: offer condolences
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: propose a toast
points.note: Untaught, and arguably not a Kannada A1 move at all; recorded rather than silently dropped.

points.label: wish somebody well
points.note: aashiirvaada ('a blessing') and vandane ('a salutation') are taught in chapter 51 as the vocabulary of well-wishing, though not as a formula.

points.label: open a conversation
points.note: Greet, then ask how they are -- the chapter 1 and 3 pair, which is the whole opening of an A1 exchange.

points.label: show you are following
points.note: sari, haage and kuuda are all available as backchannel.

points.label: move the conversation on
points.note: haagaadare and aameele, chapter 64.

points.label: close the conversation
points.note: The chapter-4 farewell, and biilkoduge ('a send-off') from chapter 50.

points.label: ask somebody to repeat or speak slowly
points.note: UNTAUGHT, and it is the single most useful sentence an A1 speaker owns. Kannada needs innondu sala heeli ('say it once more'); nothing in the corpus builds it, though heelu ('to say') is itself absent too.

points.label: parts of the body: head and hand
points.note: tale and kai, chapter 13.

points.label: parts of the body: face
points.note: kannu, baayi, kivi and muugu, one per lesson in chapter 37.

points.label: parts of the body: limbs and torso
points.note: kaalu, hallu, kuudalu, beralu and hotte, chapter 47.

points.label: parts of the body: back, neck, shoulder, lip, bone
points.note: chapter 57. Kannada's body vocabulary is unusually deep for A1 -- four chapters and eighteen words.

points.label: the heart, as organ and as feeling
points.note: hrudaya, chapter 38.

points.label: physical characteristics of a person
points.note: Untaught. dodda and cikka are taught of things; no lesson applies a quality to a person, and there is no word for tall, short, young or beautiful.

points.label: actions and positions of the body
points.note: kulituko and nillu, chapter 43.

points.label: character and personality
points.note: Untaught as description. Chapter 65 teaches the abstract nouns -- saujanya (courtesy), nambike (trust), sankoca (hesitancy) -- but nothing that describes a person with them.

points.label: personal data: name and age
points.note: hesaru and vayassu. Address, telephone and documents are all untaught.

points.label: documents: passport, identity card
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: personal objects
points.note: pustaka (book), kode (umbrella) and batte (cloth).

points.label: family: parents and siblings
points.note: appa, amma and the four age-graded sibling words -- anna, tamma, akka, tangi -- taught together in chapter 12, because Kannada will not let you say 'brother' without saying which.

points.label: family: the collective word
points.note: kutumba, chapter 35 -- the word chapter 12's people never needed until now.

points.label: family: children
points.note: magu, maga and magalu -- one root, three endings, chapter 36.

points.label: family: grandparents and spouse
points.note: ajja, ajji, ganda and hendati, chapter 45.

points.label: social relationships: friend, guest
points.note: snehita and atithi.

points.label: celebrations and occasions
points.note: rangooli and huumaale are taught in chapter 52 as the furniture of a welcome, which is the nearest the corpus comes to an occasion.

points.label: meals
points.note: uuta ('a meal'), chapter 40.

points.label: drink: water, milk, tea, coffee
points.note: niiru, haalu, cahaa and kaaphi -- chapters 15 and 39, the last two with their travel histories through Persian and Arabic.

points.label: staple foodstuffs
points.note: akki/anna plus mosaru, tuppa, enne, bella and sakkare -- chapter 61 is a South Indian kitchen shelf.

points.label: fruit and salt
points.note: hannu and uppu, chapter 46.

points.label: dishes, courses and the restaurant
points.note: Untaught. The ingredients are there and the meal is named; ordering one is not.

points.label: education: who is in the room
points.note: shikshaka and vidyaarthi, chapter 48.

points.label: education: institutions, timetable, examinations
points.note: Untaught. No word for school, class, lesson or examination.

points.label: learning and teaching as activities
points.note: oodu, bare and arthamaadiko, chapter 33.

points.label: classroom language
points.note: Untaught. See KA-A1-F-50 -- the learner cannot ask for a repetition.

points.label: teaching materials
points.note: pustaka. Nothing else -- no pen, paper, board or desk.

points.label: professions
points.note: shikshaka, vidyaarthi, vaidya and raita, chapter 48.

points.label: working activity
points.note: kelasa maadu ('to work'), taught in chapter 5 as the model noun-plus-maadu verb.

points.label: workplaces, tools, work clothing
points.note: Untaught as a domain, though chapter 62's made things (rope, needle, thread, broom, basket) and chapter 66's field words come close.

points.label: unemployment, rights at work
points.note: Untaught, and arguably above A1 in any track; recorded for completeness.

points.label: free time, sport, games, shows
points.note: Untaught, entirely. Four Spanish points and not one Kannada word -- no play, no game, no music, no film.

points.label: communication media, telephone, internet
points.note: Untaught, entirely. The corpus has no telephone, which also removes the standard A1 task of giving a number.

points.label: written correspondence
points.note: bare ('to write') only. No letter, no address, no form.

points.label: housing: parts of a dwelling
points.note: baagilu ('a door'). Chapter 56 is named HOUSE but teaches its contents rather than its rooms.

points.label: household objects and furniture
points.note: kurci, caape, butti, caaku, paatre and pettige -- chapters 52 and 56.

points.label: household made things
points.note: nuulu, suuji, hagga, porake and kode, chapter 62.

points.label: domestic activities, buying and renting a home
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: light in the house
points.note: diipa ('a lamp'), chapter 46 -- a word that carries more cultural weight in Kannada than 'lamp' does in English.

points.label: postal, financial, health and security services
points.note: Untaught, entirely.

points.label: shopping: places, people, activities
points.note: Untaught. No shop, no market, no shopkeeper.

points.label: clothing
points.note: batte ('cloth') only -- the material, not a garment. No shirt, sari or shoe.

points.label: payment and money
points.note: Untaught. No word for money, price or rupee -- so nothing can be bought, which removes a whole standard A1 task type.

points.label: health and illness
points.note: hasivu, nidde, jvara, noovu and aarogya -- chapter 63 gives hunger, sleep, fever, pain and health.

points.label: centres of health care, medicine, hygiene
points.note: vaidya ('a doctor') and nothing else -- no hospital, no medicine.

points.label: travel: setting out and the journey
points.note: prayaana and horadu, chapter 50.

points.label: the transport system and accommodation
points.note: Untaught. No bus, train, road-vehicle or hotel.

points.label: commerce, industry, energy
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: the notion of number
points.note: Numbers to twenty, plus the digits.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: government, politics, law
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: artistic disciplines, music, literature, cinema
points.note: Untaught, entirely -- six Spanish points and no Kannada word, which is a striking gap for a language whose literature the corpus itself keeps citing.

points.label: religion
points.note: aashiirvaada ('a blessing') is the only word in this domain.

points.label: the sky and its bodies
points.note: aakaasha, bisilu, candra, cukki and mooda, chapter 53.

points.label: geography: country, town, city
points.note: Untaught apart from halli ('a village'). See KA-A1-N-02.

points.label: rural space
points.note: Chapters 55 and 66 between them give river, tank, hill, village, path, field, grass, paddy, crop and harvest. This is the best-covered domain in the whole inventory, and it is a rural one -- the corpus teaches the Karnataka countryside far better than it teaches a city.

points.label: weather and climate
points.note: havaamaana ('weather') and the four seasons, including the monsoon.

points.label: elements: wind, fire, water, earth
points.note: gaali, manju, maralu, kesaru and benki, chapter 59.

points.label: fauna
points.note: naayi and bekku from chapter 21, then hasu, meeke, kooli, kaage and hakki from chapter 60.

points.label: flora
points.note: mara, kombe, ele, beeru, biija and huuvu.

points.label: colour
points.note: kappu, bili, kempu, niili from chapter 11, then hasiru and haladi from chapter 22 -- six colours.

points.label: the days of the week
points.note: All seven, chapter 10.

points.label: the months
points.note: All twelve lunisolar months, chapter 16 -- with the honest note that this is not the calendar Kannada speakers use for everyday dates.

points.label: parts of the day
points.note: belagge, sanje, aparaahna, madhyaahna and madhyaraatri -- chapters 17 and 26-28.

points.label: telling the clock
points.note: gante ('hour') and the frame that uses it, chapter 18.

points.label: sight and hearing
points.note: noodu and keelu -- and keelu is taught doing double duty as both 'hear' and 'ask'.

points.label: age as a quality
points.note: vayassu for a person, haleya for a thing, and chapter 42 is careful that haleya is not used of people.

points.label: open and closed, way in and way out
points.note: baagilu ('a door') is the only word here; neither 'open' nor 'closed' is taught.

points.label: value, price, attractiveness
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: interest, ease and difficulty
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: the script is a syllabary, not an alphabet: every consonant carries an inherent a
points.note: The founding fact, taught inside chapter 1's first letter lesson and re-stated with every consonant since.

points.label: vowel signs replace the inherent vowel
points.note: Six vowel signs have their own lessons -- u, i, e, aa, o, oo -- each taught as a mark that REPLACES the a rather than adding to it.

points.label: independent vowel letters, for word-initial position
points.note: i, u, uu, ii and oo are taught as standing letters, and the corpus is careful to pair each with the vowel sign it matches.

points.label: the virama, and the conjunct it makes
points.note: The single most important orthographic fact in the script, and it has its own lesson in chapter 3: strip a vowel and the consonant stacks UNDER the next one. Kannada calls the result ottakshara, and chapter 1's recap names it.

points.label: the anusvara and the visarga
points.note: Both marks that ride a letter rather than sitting beside it, taught in chapters 14 and 38.

points.label: consonant letters: the taught set
points.note: Twenty-two consonants have their own one-glyph lesson across the track, arriving one at a time behind a word the learner already says.

points.label: the aspirated series
points.note: jha and tha are taught explicitly as the breathed partners of ja and ta -- the pattern rather than two more shapes.

points.label: the written digits
points.note: All ten, one per chapter across 9-18. Probed here on the endpoints; the full set is at KA-A1-NUM-03.

points.label: THE SCRIPT IS NOT CLOSED: 27 characters are used but never taught
points.note: MEASURED, AND THE LARGEST SINGLE FINDING IN THIS COLUMN. The corpus teaches 42 Kannada characters and USES 69 distinct ones in headwords -- 61% closure. The 27 untaught characters are not exotic: ma appears in 40 headwords, la in 37, va in 30, ta in 20, ja in 16. A learner who has done every script lesson still cannot read maatanaaDu, the verb chapter 5 is built on. Do not assume the Tamil shape here: Tamil's script column came back 52 of 52 taught, and Kannada's is the opposite case.

points.label: capital letters
points.note: Untransferable, and recorded rather than dropped: Kannada has no letter case at all. Nothing to teach.

points.label: written accentuation
points.note: Untransferable. Kannada writes no accent; vowel length is a different letter or a different sign, which KA-A1-L-02 and KA-A1-L-03 cover instead.

points.label: the full stop and the comma
points.note: Untaught. Modern Kannada uses the Latin full stop and comma, and the older danda; no lesson mentions punctuation at all.

points.label: the question mark
points.note: Untaught as a convention, though it is used throughout the books. Kannada does not use the inverted opening marks Spanish does.

points.label: other punctuation: colon, quotation marks, parentheses, dash
points.note: Untaught. Six Spanish points collapse here because Kannada borrows the Latin set wholesale and the corpus teaches none of it.

points.label: abbreviations, initialisms and symbols
points.note: Untaught.

points.label: superscript letters in abbreviations
points.note: Untransferable. A Spanish typographic convention with no Kannada counterpart.

points.label: the retroflex series, and that it is contrastive
points.note: Dda and lla have their own lessons. The retroflex/dental contrast is the single hardest thing about Kannada for an English speaker and the corpus does introduce the letters, though never as a minimal pair.

points.label: aspiration as a contrast
points.note: jha and tha are both taught as 'the breathed partner of' an unaspirated letter, which is the contrast stated.

points.label: vowel length is contrastive
points.note: u/uu and i/ii are taught as pairs, explicitly as long partners of short vowels.

points.label: the geminate: a held double consonant
points.note: Taught obliquely but genuinely: chapter 6 explains that the doubled -kke resisted the voicing that turned -ke into -ge, which only makes sense once gemination is understood as holding the consonant.

points.label: the p-to-h sound law that shapes modern Kannada
points.note: Chapter 2 teaches it on hesaru, and the track returns to it repeatedly. It is the fact that makes Kannada look unlike its sisters on the page. NO SPANISH ORIGIN: The p-to-h sound law. A fact about this language's history that shapes how half its everyday words look, and has no analogue in the proxy.

points.label: the anusvara as a nasal that assimilates
points.note: Chapter 14's lesson, and chapter 7's ombattu, which is taught as 'one mark, whichever nasal the next letter needs'.

points.label: word stress and intonation
points.note: Untaught. Kannada stress is weakly initial and rarely contrastive, but no lesson says so, and question intonation is never described.

points.label: the respect grade in the second person
points.note: Taught twice and taught as a rule rather than a pair of words: respect is the plural, and the verb ending must match the pronoun.

points.label: when a politeness word is actually used, and when it is not
points.note: The corpus is unusually careful here: dayavittu and kshamisi both carry a pragmatics atom saying that Kannada speakers reach for these less often than an English speaker expects. That is register taught as behaviour, not vocabulary.

points.label: greetings that are formal, and the everyday alternative
points.note: Three pragmatics atoms across chapters 26-31 say plainly that shubhoodaya and its siblings are more written than spoken, and that namaskaara covers most of the day.

points.label: the spoken/literary divide itself
points.note: UNTAUGHT AS A NAMED FACT, and this is the column core/exam-levels.json does not warn about. Kannada is as diglossic as Tamil -- a literary grandhika register and an everyday aaDubhaashe that differ in verb endings and pronouns -- but where Tamil's exam-levels entry carries an explicit diglossia caveat, Kannada's carries none. The corpus does in fact teach the spoken variety consistently: all 249 schema-v2 lessons declare variety: standard-colloquial, which is a real and uniform editorial choice. What no lesson does is TELL the learner that a different register exists, so a reader meeting written Kannada will not know why it looks unfamiliar. Recommended: one lesson, and a caveat added to exam-levels.json. NO SPANISH ORIGIN: The spoken/literary divide. Diglossia is not a dimension the Spanish inventory has any reason to enumerate.

points.label: distributive: one ... the other
points.note: Untaught, and downstream of everything else in this column: Kannada builds it on ondu ... innondu, and innondu is absent. Recorded so the proxy's distributive point is attributed rather than quietly dropped.

points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Untaught. Kannada would use suumne iri or the imperative of a verb of silence; neither the verb nor the construction is in the corpus.
